rows.name: Draw a square from the class's spoken instructions
steps: Educator stands at the board and draws a square only as the children's spoken instructions say.
If a child says 'Draw a line', draw a messy squiggle.
If a child says 'Turn', turn around in a circle.
Children see that clear distances and exact turns are needed and restate their instructions.
rows.materials: Board and marker (not named in the plan).

levels.0: The steps are vague, such as 'draw a line', and a partner cannot follow them.
levels.1: The steps are in order but a distance or a turn is missing until a partner asks.
levels.2: The written steps are in exact order with distances and turns, so a partner can follow them.
levels.3: The steps are corrected and shortened after a partner follows them, and the child gives the reason for each change.

rows.note: Precise Algorithms; materials not stated in cell.

rows.name: Scratch: connect Green Flag to Move 50 Steps
steps: Open the full Scratch interface.
Practise drag-and-dropping blocks into the programming panel.
Connect 'When Green Flag Clicked' to the blue 'Move 50 Steps' block.
Change the step count and watch how the on-screen distance changes in proportion.

levels.0: The blocks are not joined and the sprite does not move.
levels.1: The sprite moves after the educator helps join the blocks.
levels.2: The sprite moves when the green flag is clicked and the child changes the step count on purpose.
levels.3: The child predicts the distance for a new step count and then checks it on screen.

rows.name: Human Keyboard
steps: When the educator claps once (input), the whole room shouts 'Beep!' (output).
When the educator stomps a foot (input), the whole room jumps up (output).
Children tell which action was the input and which the output.

levels.0: The child does not link the signal to the response.
levels.1: The child answers to the signals after watching others.
levels.2: The child answers correctly to each signal and names the input and the output.
levels.3: The child makes up a new input and output pair for the game and explains it.

rows.name: Scratch: keyboard controls for a sprite
steps: Connect the 'When Space Key Pressed' block to a sound effect.
Set up 'When Right Arrow Key Pressed' to move the sprite 10 steps along the positive X-axis.
Press the keys and check the sprite and sound respond.

levels.0: Pressing the keys does nothing because no key block is joined.
levels.1: The controls work after the educator helps with one block.
levels.2: Pressing the space key makes the sound and the right arrow moves the sprite 10 steps.
levels.3: The child adds a second key control of their own and says which part is the input and which the output.

rows.name: Flipbook animation demonstration
rows.unit: The World of Animation and Changing Sprites
steps: Show the class a simple 3-page paper flipbook of a stick figure waving.
Flip the pages quickly.
Talk about how changing frames makes it look alive.

levels.0: The child does not link the moving look to the changing pictures.
levels.1: The child says the figure moves after the educator points to the changing pages.
levels.2: The child explains that fast-changing pictures make the figure seem to move.
levels.3: The child explains why too slow or too fast a flip spoils the movement.

rows.name: Scratch: walking animation with Next Costume and Wait
rows.unit: The World of Animation and Changing Sprites
steps: Choose a sprite from the library with at least three costumes, such as a walking person.
Loop 'Next Costume' blocks.
Put a 'Wait 0.2 Seconds' block between each change.
Run it and see a smooth walking motion.

levels.0: The costume does not change on screen.
levels.1: The sprite changes costume but jerkily until the educator helps with the wait block.
levels.2: The sprite walks smoothly using Next Costume with 0.2-second waits.
levels.3: The child changes the wait time and explains what happens to the walking speed.

rows.name: Jumping jacks: write it long or short
steps: Ask children to do 5 jumping jacks, counting aloud 1 to 5.
Write two versions on the board: 'Jumping Jack' written 5 times, and 'Repeat 5 Times: [Jumping Jack]'.
Ask which saves the most time and board space.

levels.0: The child does not tell the two versions apart.
levels.1: The child chooses the repeat version after a prompt.
levels.2: The child chooses the repeat version and says it saves time and space.
levels.3: The child writes a repeat version for another action of their own.

rows.name: Scratch: squeeze four moves and turns into Repeat 4
steps: Start from a long script of 'Move 10 steps' and 'Turn 90 degrees' four times.
Replace it with one clean 'Repeat 4' block.
Run both to check they give the same result.

levels.0: The script still repeats the blocks by hand and has no loop.
levels.1: The loop works after the educator helps place the blocks inside Repeat.
levels.2: The long script is replaced by one Repeat 4 block with the same result.
levels.3: The child makes a loop for a new shape and explains the count they chose.

rows.name: Maze: test the messy script step by step
steps: Draw a complex maze with dead ends on the board.
Write a long messy script beside it with two errors put in.
Trace the path step by step with a finger to find where the script loses the route.

levels.0: The child cannot find where the script goes wrong.
levels.1: The child finds one error with help.
levels.2: The child traces the script and points to where it goes wrong.
levels.3: The child finds both errors and says how to correct each.

rows.name: Clear and Concise Programs challenge
steps: Hand out an intentionally messy, over-long block sequence for a sprite.
Children analyse the logic.
Remove redundant or conflicting blocks and rebuild with fewer blocks.
Check the output stays exactly the same.

levels.0: The script still has the conflicting blocks or the output changed.
levels.1: The script is shorter after help from the educator, with the same output.
levels.2: The script has fewer blocks and the output is the same.
levels.3: The child tells which blocks were redundant and why removing them is safe.

source.cell: 2. Stratified Practical Lab — Grade 3 Pathway (Practical Task)

rows.name: Plus/Delta feedback
steps: Explain that software engineers share their work to get feedback.
Discuss how to give polite feedback.
Use Plus/Delta: one thing that works well and one suggestion for improvement.

levels.0: The child does not give feedback on another's work.
levels.1: The child gives a 'plus' only, or needs a prompt for the 'delta'.
levels.2: The child gives one 'plus' and one 'delta' in a polite way.
levels.3: The child makes the 'delta' specific and says how it would help.

rows.note: No LO in the G3 set is about giving feedback; coordinator may add one.

rows.name: Scratch: interactive greeting card or short animated story
steps: Create an interactive greeting card or short animated story.
Make the background stage change when specific input triggers are used.
Keep the blocks clean and readable.
Write step-by-step instructions on how a user should use it (e.g., press space to start).

levels.0: The project has no working input trigger.
levels.1: The project works with help for one trigger.
levels.2: The project changes the background stage with an input and the blocks are readable.
levels.3: The child adds a feature of their own and explains how the blocks produce it.
